finding: The asteroid belt has narrow, nearly empty lanes at fixed distances from the Sun.
key_numbers: 2.48-2.52 AU: 9,123 asteroids where a smooth belt would have about 72,260 (0.13); dips found by code at 2.07, 2.50, 2.82, 2.95, 3.29 AU
how_checked: split numbered/unnumbered; bin widths 0.005/0.01/0.02 AU; compared with a smooth-belt expectation
reasons: Data proves: the dips are in both halves and at every bin width. Known science (outside the data): Jupiter goes round the Sun every 11.862 years; by Kepler's law (per_y = a^1.5, which the file follows, Step 1) the dips sit where an asteroid would go round a whole number of times per Jupiter orbit: 2.07 AU -> 3.97 orbits per Jupiter orbit, 2.50 AU -> 2.99 orbits per Jupiter orbit, 2.82 AU -> 2.50 orbits per Jupiter orbit, 2.96 AU -> 2.34 orbits per Jupiter orbit, 3.29 AU -> 1.98 orbits per Jupiter orbit. Jupiter's pull repeats at the same spot every time, and clears these lanes (the Kirkwood gaps).
tip: Teacher: show chart A05 and ask students to compute a^1.5 at each dip and divide 11.86 by it; the whole-number ratios appear by themselves.

finding: Three separate groups sit outside the main belt, at about 1.9, 4.0 and 5.2 AU.
key_numbers: peak bins at 1.91 AU; 3.95 AU; 5.20 AU
how_checked: found as peaks on the chart; positions read by code
reasons: Data proves: the three bumps are separate from the main belt (A05) and two of them sit at high tilt or in their own band (A09). Known science (outside the data): the group at 4.0 AU (Hildas) goes round the Sun 3 times for every 2 Jupiter orbits, and the 5.2 AU group (Trojans) shares Jupiter's orbit; these rhythms protect them instead of clearing them. The 1.9 AU group (Hungarias) is tilted by about 20 degrees, which keeps it away from Mars.

finding: Past Neptune, objects pile up in a narrow band at 39.2-39.7 AU.
key_numbers: 601 objects in 39.2-39.7 AU against about 171 expected from the side windows (3.5x)
how_checked: split numbered/unnumbered; shifted bins by 0.125 AU; compared with side windows
reasons: Data proves: the spike is in both halves and survives shifted bins. Known science (outside the data): an orbit at 39.4 AU takes about 248 years, 1.50 times Neptune's 164.8-year orbit, so these objects go round twice for every three Neptune orbits, as Pluto does (the 'Plutinos'). That rhythm keeps them from ever meeting Neptune.

finding: The main belt contains tight clumps of asteroids that share almost the same distance and tilt.
key_numbers: 12 clumps, the strongest at a 2.868 AU, i 1.2 deg, 3.0x denser than around it
how_checked: same finder on numbered only (9/12 found again) and unnumbered only (11/12); coarser cells (11/12)
reasons: Data proves: the same clumps appear in two separate halves of the data and with bigger cells. Known science (outside the data): asteroid families are pieces of one parent body broken in a collision; the pieces keep similar orbits. The clump at about 2.87 AU and 2 degrees matches the known Koronis family, and the one at 2.64 AU and 13 degrees the Eunomia family. Guess: the other clumps are other families; not checked against a family catalogue.
tip: Astronomy club or teacher: chart A09 is a good 'find the families' exercise; each dark clump is the debris of one broken rock.

finding: Asteroids get darker the farther they orbit from the Sun.
how_checked: split by size (both halves fall); moved zone edges by 0.05 AU; checked how many have an albedo in each zone
reasons: Data proves: the fall is there for big and small asteroids and does not depend on the exact zone edges. Known science (outside the data): the inner belt is mostly stony (bright) asteroids and the outer belt mostly carbon-rich (dark) ones. The spike at 1.90 AU (median 0.54) is the Hungaria group, known for very bright surfaces. Caution (data proves): only 7% / 8% / 11% / 14% of asteroids in the four zones have an albedo, mostly the bigger ones.
tip: Anyone turning H into a size: the usual albedo 0.14 is too bright for the outer belt (median 0.066 at 2.82-3.3 AU), which makes those sizes 1.46 times too small. Use the zone medians from numbers/A10_albedo_zones.csv instead.

finding: Asteroids bigger than about 300 m almost never spin faster than once every 2.2 hours, but most smaller than 150 m do.
key_numbers: > 0.3 km: 1,236 of 33,616 fast (3.7%; 2.2% with measured sizes only); < 0.15 km: 524 of 655 (80%)
how_checked: changed size cut (0.25/0.4 km) and period cut (2.0/2.4 h); measured sizes only
reasons: Data proves: the floor at 2.2 h holds for every cut-off tried and with measured sizes only. Known science (outside the data): most asteroids bigger than a few hundred metres are loose piles of rubble held together only by their weak gravity; spinning faster than about 2.2 hours would throw material off their equator. Small ones can be single solid rocks, which can spin much faster. Guess: many of the 1,236 exceptions have wrong sizes (sizes from H assume albedo 0.14) or wrong periods; not tested here.
tip: Mission planner: a target under 150 m will most likely spin in minutes, not hours; plan the approach and any landing for that.

finding: 2025 has three times more first sightings than a normal recent year, most of them in July 2025.
how_checked: split by kind; compared with 2018-2024; checked partial dates and how the days spread inside July
reasons: Data proves: the jump is real in the file and almost all unnumbered (new) objects; 58% of July sits in 3 days. Known science (outside the data): the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile released its first images in June 2025 and began reporting large numbers of new asteroids. Guess: the July 2025 batch is the first data of a new deep survey, reported in a few big submissions; the file cannot say which telescope saw them.
tip: Science journalist: '2025 broke the record' is true for recent years only; 2005 has more first sightings (next finding).

finding: The busiest year for first sightings is 2005, not 2025: first_obs is not the discovery year.
how_checked: split by kind; compared decades; file's own definition of first_obs
reasons: Data proves: older first sightings are mostly numbered objects (long known), recent ones are none. Known science (outside the data): large surveys from the late 1990s onward photographed huge numbers of faint asteroids; when an asteroid is found later, those older images are matched to it and become its first observation. Guess: this back-filling is why 2000-2015 look so busy and recent years look quieter; recent objects have not been matched to old images yet.
tip: Anyone using this file: never call first_obs the discovery year; it moves back in time as old images are matched.

finding: A few single days hold thousands of first sightings each.
how_checked: compared with a normal day; looked at what the objects are
reasons: Data proves: on 2014-04-23 the objects are 97% unnumbered and have few observations (median 19). Guess: each spike is one very deep night of one big telescope whose images were later searched for asteroids; it is a bias of how the data was collected, not an event in space.
tip: Data analysts: check single-day spikes before reading any trend from first_obs; group by month or year.

finding: Newly found near-Earth asteroids get much smaller over time.
how_checked: split numbered/unnumbered; 25th percentile instead of median; the size formula cannot create a trend
reasons: Data proves: H rises (fainter, smaller) in both halves and in the brightest quarter, and fewer and fewer kilometre-sized ones are new each decade. Known science (outside the data): survey telescopes keep getting more sensitive; the big near-Earth asteroids were found first, so new finds are mostly small ones.
tip: Planetary-defence communicator: the record numbers of new near-Earth asteroids are mostly small rocks; new kilometre-sized ones are now rare.

finding: Jupiter's Trojans form two clumps 120 degrees apart, and the leading clump has about 1.8 times more members.
key_numbers: 10,494 vs 5,951 (ratio 1.76); bright only (H < 13): 927 vs 631 (1.47); 35 standard deviations from equal
how_checked: split by brightness; moved the split lines by 10 degrees; compared with an even split
reasons: Data proves: the clumps are 120 degrees apart and unequal in bright and faint halves. Known science (outside the data): Trojans collect around two balance points 60 degrees ahead of and behind Jupiter; Jupiter sits halfway between them (here about 118 degrees), and the bigger clump at 178 degrees is the one ahead of Jupiter. The leading swarm is known to be larger; why is still argued about. Guess: the smaller ratio for bright Trojans (1.47) means part of the gap among faint ones comes from how well each swarm has been searched.
tip: Teacher: chart A14 is a clean picture of Lagrange points, the same balance points where space telescopes are parked.

finding: The 'potentially hazardous' and 'near-Earth' flags are formulas of other columns, not separate judgements.
key_numbers: pha: 2,517 of 2,550 match moid <= 0.05 and H <= 22, all 2,550 with H <= 22.6; neo = Y: 99.97% have q < 1.3
how_checked: rebuilt both rules from the columns; moved the H and q cut-offs
reasons: Data proves: the flags can be rebuilt from moid, H and q. Known science (outside the data): NASA defines a potentially hazardous asteroid as moid of 0.05 AU or less and H of 22 or less, and a near-Earth object as q below 1.3 AU. Guess: the 33 exceptions (H 22.01 to 22.57) had H of 22 or less when they were flagged and their H was updated later.
tip: Machine-learning team: a model that predicts pha from moid and H only relearns this rule and will look perfect; leave those columns out or predict something else.

finding: Counts of asteroids fall off for H fainter than about 18; this is where surveys stop seeing them, not a real shortage.
key_numbers: peak H 17.5-18; numbered peak 17, unnumbered 18; near-Earth median H 24.1
how_checked: split numbered/unnumbered; compared with near-Earth asteroids, which are seen closer
reasons: Data proves: the peak moves with the group (numbered vs unnumbered), and asteroids that come close to Earth are found much fainter. Known science (outside the data): small asteroids are far more common than big ones; faint ones are missed because they are too dim to detect far away.
tip: Anyone counting asteroids: the shape after the peak tells you about the telescopes, not about the asteroids.

finding: Orbits that go round 'backwards' (tilt above 90 degrees) are almost all comets.
key_numbers: 2,381 with i > 90; 2,173 (91%) are unnumbered comets; asteroids: 201
reasons: Data proves: most backwards orbits are comets. Known science (outside the data): long-period comets fall in from the far-away Oort cloud from every direction, so their tilts are random; asteroids formed in the flat disc around the Sun and stay near it.

finding: Numbered asteroids have very certain orbits; a third of the unnumbered ones have very uncertain orbits.
reasons: Data proves: the split by kind. Known science (outside the data): an asteroid only gets a number once its orbit is well measured, usually over several years, so numbering and orbit quality go together.
tip: Orbit researchers: filter to condition_code of 5 or less before studying orbit shapes, or the uncertain ones blur the picture.
